q-4868:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=4.9$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(4.9)+{f}^{′}(4.9)(x-4.9) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+5(x-4.9).\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(5)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=5.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(5) & ≈L(5) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+5(5-4.9) \\  & =0.5+5(0.1) \\  & =0.5+0.5 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

q-115593:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(\frac{\pi }{4})+{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})(x-\frac{\pi }{4}).\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $f(\frac{\pi }{4})=0,$ and since ${f}^{′}(x)=\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{sec}⁡x,$ then ${f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})=\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=2.$ So, the tangent line approximation is given by

$$
L(x)=2(x-\frac{\pi }{4}).
$$

Now, we can approximate $f(1)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1) & ≈L(1) \\  & =2(1-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =2-\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-4814:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(1)+{f}^{′}(1)(x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $f(1)=-2,$ and since ${f}^{′}(x)=12{x}^{2}-6,$ then ${f}^{′}(1)=12(1)^{2}-6=6.$ So, the tangent line approximation is given by

$$
L(x)=-2+6(x-1).
$$

Now, we can approximate $f(2)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=2.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2) & ≈L(2) \\  & =-2+6(2-1) \\  & =-2+6(1) \\  & =-2+6 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

q-115265:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=1$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(1)+{f}^{′}(1)(x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

The function passes through the point $(1,2),$ so we have $f(1)=2.$ Also, we're told that ${f}^{′}(1)=-2,$ so we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =2+(-2)(x-1) \\  & =2-2(x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $f(0.8)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=0.8.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0.8) & ≈L(0.8) \\  & =2-2(0.8-1) \\  & =2-2(-0.2) \\  & =2.4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the function is concave up on the interval $(0,2),$ the linear approximation $L(x)$ is below the graph close to $x=1,$ and therefore we have an underestimate.

q-346720:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $a=0$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a) \\  & =f(0)+{f}^{′}(0)(x-0).\end{aligned}
$$

The graph of the function passes through the point $(0,2),$ so we have $f(0)=2.$ Also, we're told that ${f}^{′}(0)=0.5.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x) & =2+0.5x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can approximate $f(0.4)$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=0.4.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0.4) & ≈L(0.4) \\  & =2+0.5(0.4) \\  & =2.2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the function is concave down on the interval $(-2,2),$ the linear approximation $L(x)$ is above the graph near $x=0,$ and therefore we have an $\text{overestimate}.$

q-128382:
First, from the equation of the plane we get that the normal vector of $Π$ is $n=⟨3,5,0⟩.$

Now, we solve the Cartesian equation of $Π$ for $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+5y+15 & =0 \\ 5y & =-3x-15 \\ y & =-\frac{3}{5}x-3.\end{aligned}
$$

If we put, say, $x=0$, we get $y=-3.$ Hence, the point $P(0,-3,0)$ lies on $Π.$ Note that the position vector of $P$ is $p=⟨0,-3,0⟩.$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ (r-⟨0,-3,0⟩)\cdot ⟨3,5,0⟩ & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

q-336218:
First, we note that the position vector of $P$ is $p=⟨0,2,3⟩.$ From the Cartesian equation, we find that the line is parallel to the vector $⟨0,-5,4⟩.$ So, the normal vector of the plane is 

$$
n=⟨0,-5,4⟩.
$$

Using the dot product, we can find the equation of the plane as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(r-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ r\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ r\cdot ⟨0,-5,4⟩ & =⟨0,2,3⟩\cdot ⟨0,-5,4⟩ \\ r\cdot ⟨0,-5,4⟩ & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to obtain the Cartesian equation of the plane, we substitute $r=⟨x,y,z⟩$ into the equation above and get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨0,-5,4⟩ & =2 \\ -5y+4z & =2 \\ -5y+4z-2 & =0 \\ 5y-4z+2 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

q-74650:
The augmented matrix for this system is 

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}2 & 6 & 4 \\ 1 & k+1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Using the method of Gaussian elimination, we can reduce this matrix to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 6 & 4 \\ 1 & k+1 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 6 & 4 \\ 0 & k-2 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

The corresponding system is now 

$$
{\begin{aligned} & 2x+6y=4 \\  & (k-2)y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is consistent dependent if it has infinitely many solutions. For the system to have infinitely many solutions, it must have at least one free variable.

If $k=2,$ then the second equation is $0=0,$ which is true for any value of $y.$ So, we can remove this equation from the system. As a result, the system will contain only one equation, $2x+6y=4.$  

Then, the basic variable will be $x,$ and we will have a free variable $y.$ That means the system will have infinitely many solutions.

Therefore, our system is consistent dependent when $k=2.$

q-131720:
To classify the system, we first need to find its solution. The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}2 & -6 & -2 & 4 \\ 3 & -9 & -3 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

Using the method of Gaussian elimination, we can reduce this matrix to row echelon form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -6 & -2 & 4 \\ 3 & -9 & -3 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & -1 & 2 \\ 3 & -9 & -3 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x,$ and we have two free variables, $y$ and $z.$ That means we can find $x$ in terms of $y$ and $z.$ 

Therefore, since there are infinitely many solutions, we conclude that the system is *consistent dependent*. 

As a result, only statement III is true.

q-75519:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{e}^{t}\,,\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t}\,,\,\frac{t}{\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors  $⟨0\,,\,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular for some value of the parameter $t$ if and only if $⟨0\,,\,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t)=0.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨0\,,\,1⟩\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ⟨0\,,\,1⟩\cdot ⟨{e}^{t}\,,\,\frac{t}{\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}}⟩ & =0 \\ 0\cdot {e}^{t}+1\cdot \frac{t}{\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}} & =0 \\ \frac{t}{\sqrt{1+{t}^{2}}} & =0 \\ t & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only solution is $t=0.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨{e}^{0}\,,\,\sqrt{1+{0}^{2}}⟩=⟨1\,,\,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨0\,,\,1⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are perpendicular at the point $(1,1).$

q-165039:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}+4t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}+9t)⟩ \\  & =⟨3t+4,6t+9⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c⟨1,3⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c⟨1,3⟩ \\ ⟨3t+4,6t+9⟩ & =c⟨1,3⟩ \\ ⟨3t+4,6t+9⟩ & =⟨c,3c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
{\begin{aligned}3t+4=c \\ 6t+9=3c\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $c=3t+4.$ Substituting $c=3t+4$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6t+9 & =3(3t+4) \\ 6t+9 & =9t+12 \\ 3t & =-3 \\ t & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $⟨1,3⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=-1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨\frac{3}{2}(-1)^{2}+4(-1),3(-1)^{2}+9(-1)⟩=⟨-\frac{5}{2},-6⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨1,3⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(-\frac{5}{2},-6).$

q-114016:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{3}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can split up the given integral using the sum rule and factor out the constants. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{3}(8-f(x))\,\text{d}x & =8{\int }_{1}^{3}\text{d}x-{\int }_{1}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =8\cdot x\,{|}_{1}^{3}-6 \\  & =8(3-1)-6 \\  & =8\cdot 2-6 \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

q-73342:
From the adjacent intervals rule, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{-1}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-2}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in the known information into the above gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}+2={\int }_{-2}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{5}{2}={\int }_{-2}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we compute the desired integral and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{1}(5+4f(x))\,\text{d}x & =5{\int }_{-2}^{1}\,\text{d}x+4{\int }_{-2}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\cdot x\,{|}_{-2}^{1}+4(\frac{5}{2}) \\  & =5(1-(-2))+10 \\  & =25.\end{aligned}
$$

q-114153:
Let's simplify one of the given integrals:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{1}\frac{1}{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =2 \\ \frac{1}{3}{\int }_{4}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =2 \\ -\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =2 \\ {\int }_{1}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Then, from the adjacent intervals rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =6+(-6) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

q-4726:
Let's simplify one of the given integrals:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{7}\frac{1}{2}\,g(x)\,\text{d}x & =5 \\ \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{7}g(x)\,\text{d}x & =5 \\ {\int }_{0}^{7}g(x)\,\text{d}x & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the adjacent intervals rule and substituting the known values, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{7}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x+{\int }_{3}^{7}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x \\ {\int }_{0}^{7}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by applying the sum rule for definite integrals and substituting the known values, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{7}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x+4 \\ {\int }_{0}^{7}f(x)\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{0}^{7}g(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x+4 \\ 18-10 & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x+4 \\ 4 & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${\int }_{0}^{3}(f(x)-g(x))\text{d}x=4.$
